newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU enlargement could shatter EU political scene.
newsitem.headline: EU enlargement could shatter EU political scene.

text.p: European Union enlargement to Central and Eastern Europe could shatter the traditional political makeup of the European Parliament, the leader of the European Christian Democrats said on Tuesday.

"Either the three big parties (in the European Parliament) will succeed in attracting a large majority of the public in the new EU member states or the European political landscape will dissolve," Wilfred Martens told Reuters.

Many of the battalion of small parties angling for power in the former Soviet bloc countries have platforms which do not slip easily into the moulds offered by the three traditional political families in the European Parliament -- Socialists, Christian Democrats and Liberals.

Martens' European Peoples' Party (EPP), the second largest group in the European Parliament, is actively seeking stronger ties with parties in the nine states seeking EU membership, in a bid to make the EPP the main political force in an enlarged EU.

The only condition for joining the EPP, according to Martens, is that these parties should be committed both to traditional Christian Democrat values, including a market economy, and to a federal Europe.

The problem is that Eastern Europe is peppered with parties that favour a market economy but are fiercely nationalist and pro-European groups seeking economic reform which are led by members of the Soviet era nomenklatura.
Meanwhile, the traditional Christian Democrat parties in Eastern Europe, which were outlawed in 1947, are only now beginning to rise from the ashes.
It will be some years before they can develop political programmes of sufficient substance, according to Dutch Christian Democrat Euro-MP Wim van Velzen.

And in Hungary, the EPP's potential ally, the KDNP, has been told it will be ostracised unless it severs all links with the extreme right-wing MIEP, which is too close to the French National Front for the EPP's comfort.
Martens said the EPP was not prepared to accept this motley crew -- or indeed Eurosceptic Christian Democrats in Portugal and Scandinavia -- if it meant compromising the party's essential principles.

"We're not there to collect people," he said, accusing the European Socialist Party, the largest group in the European Parliament, of opening its arms to unreformed East European Communist parties in a bid to build up its power base.

At the same time, both Martens and Van Velzen, who chairs the EPP's parent body, the European Union of Christian Democrats (EUCD), are aware that if they can't bring these new parties into their fold, the newcomers could swell the ranks of the European Parliament's small anti-federalist groups.
These include the Europe of Nations, led by the billionaire James Goldsmith, whose Referendum Party in Britain is campaigning for a nationwide referendum on Britain's membership of the EU.

The EPP's strategy for preventing the dissolution of the EU's political scene as they know it is a campaign to teach young East European politicians how to create a political platform, explain what European integration means and give them an EPP definition of a "social market economy" -- something far removed from the Soviet era version of the term.
Though optimistic, Martens and Van Velzen accept this will take time.
"The old nomenklatura is still capable. For the next 20 years it will always have at least 20 to 30 percent of the vote because all the interest groups are dependent on them," Van Velzen said.
